author: fester
body: A literal pattern's value arrives as its source spelling. `True` and `False` are the Boolean scrutinee's 1 and 0; `parse-int-text` reads neither and answers 0 for both, so every `is True` and `is False` compared against 0 and the arms inverted. Characters were reduced to digits by the desugarer and pass through unchanged. This mirrors the compiler's `pat-lit-to-integer`; the two plugs carry their own copy because the IR text wire hands them the spelling, not the value.

author: fester
body: A read of a file on a target with no filesystem. There is no block driver behind these calls on riscv, so the compile is refused and the call is named, rather than answering the empty string: the caller named a path, got "", and could not tell that apart from an empty file. `run.ps1` fails the build on the tag.

author: fester
body: The write path is deliberately not here. `write-file` answers 0 and its callers already read that as failure, so the writes are honest; only the reads lie.

author: fester
body: The builtin-List pattern intrinsics, refused for a third reason: they are not implemented on this lane and there is no honest value to answer with. A `when` on a builtin List desugars to a length test plus __list-head and __list-tail over an O(1) tail view, and none of the three exists in the riscv runtime.

author: fester
body: Before this arm they fell through the dispatch tail to a plain call to an undefined symbol. Measured on codex/test/list-pattern: the compile reported OK and the program then printed nothing at all. That is worse than the port hole it resembles, because a length that answers garbage selects the wrong arm and the whole match is decided by it.

author: fester
body: Refusing is the honest answer while the intrinsics are unimplemented. The arms match on the name alone, no arity gate, so a partial application refuses too. codex/test/list-pattern.cross-refusal pins that the refusal fires; lose these arms and that test compiles clean and the row goes red.

author: fester
body: A literal sub-pattern inside a constructor pattern used to be DROPPED here exactly as it was on ARM64: only IrVarPat was handled and the rest fell out of the otherwise arm, so the tag was the only thing tested and `is BInt (0)` matched any BInt. Measured 2026-07-21, this lane produced the SAME eighteen wrong lines as ARM64 on codex/test/literal-subpattern. A Text literal also cannot be a bne against rv-pat-lit-to-integer: the scrutinee is a pointer, so `is "sin"` matched nothing.

author: fester
body: `rv-count-ir-locals` cannot be the guard here: it scores `IrMatch` as 2 and never looks at the branch bodies, so a match always came in under the frameless threshold. Counting it correctly would not help either, because the frameless budget for locals is not six -- it is zero.

author: fester
body: The shape this was hiding behind: a tail call under `if` allocates no local and is fine, and a NON-tail call inside a `when` arm needs `ra` and therefore gets a frame anyway. Only a TAIL call inside a `when` arm lands in the gap, which is why two working shapes sat either side of it.

author: fester
body: These two lists must agree, and a disagreement between them is a silent miscompile rather than a diagnostic. `rv-is-inline-2arg` says a name costs no call, which is what lets a tail argument holding it be treated as frameless-safe; `rv-emit-frameless-arg` is what actually has to emit it without a call. A name blessed here and unhandled there reaches the general emitter, which uses a0 and a1 -- the parameters of a frameless function -- and the loop loses its induction variable. `bit-xor` sat in exactly that gap and hung every checksum on the lane.

author: fester
body: All six bitwise operations are named in both places now, along with the two integer remainders. `bit-not` is the odd one: it takes a single argument, so it is answered by `rv-is-inline-1arg` below and lowered in the one-argument branch of `rv-emit-frameless-arg`.

author: fester
body: The bitwise arms below take the I-type immediate form when their right operand is a literal, through the same `rv-bit-imm-ok` and `rv-bit-imm-apply` the framed path uses (`RiscVCodeGen.codex`, where the defect and its bound are written down). Here the left operand is lowered by `rv-emit-frameless-arg` rather than by `rv-emit-expr`, which is the only difference and the reason the check is duplicated at each arm instead of living in one wrapper.

author: fester
body: Every argument is lowered by `rv-emit-frameless-arg` and never by `rv-emit-expr`. That is the correctness condition, and it used to hold on only one of the three paths this function had.

author: fester
body: The symptom was a hang and not a wrong answer. A two-parameter loop over a bit operation lost its induction variable, never reached its bound, and the cross harness recorded a test that produced no output at all. Pinned by selecting each branch from source: the both-read shape answered and the asymmetric shapes hung, differing in nothing else.

author: fester
body: The three paths are now one. `rv-parallel-assign-2` emits no move for a value already in the register it belongs in, so the ordering analysis the asymmetric paths existed to exploit costs little to give up, and it is not worth a second lowering path that has to be kept honest. `rv-tail-reads-reg` is still read by the framed direct path.

author: fester
body: So each argument is placed with `rv-store-local` after it is emitted. That call is free when the request was honoured, because it compares `local == value-reg` and emits nothing, and it is also the only correct move when the parameter's local is a spill slot rather than a register. `rv-emit-arg-to-param`, twenty lines above, has always done this.

author: fester
body: `rv-body-is-frameless` below is the admission test this gate was evidently meant to use, and NOTHING CALLS IT: the only references to it are its own recursion. It asks the question that matters, demanding each condition satisfy `rv-cond-is-frameless-safe` and each tail argument satisfy `rv-arg-is-frameless-safe`, where the local count here cannot express the real budget, which for callee-saved registers in a function that emits no prologue is zero rather than six.

author: fester
body: Do not simply wire it in. That was tried 2026-07-20 and it makes the lane WORSE, because a body it refuses falls to the framed path and the framed two-argument tail call is separately broken for the same shapes: `v-shru`, a two-parameter loop over `bit-shru`, answers correctly frameless and hangs framed. Both paths need to be right before the honest gate can be turned on. Measured, not reasoned.

author: fester
body: A `when` body is a tail position for each arm and an ordinary position for the scrutinee, exactly as `IrIf` is for its branches and condition. Without this arm the walk fell to `otherwise` and answered False for every match body, so a match-bodied TCO function that makes a NON-tail call in an arm (`is Cons (h) (t) -> if pred h then Cons h (f pred t) else f pred t`) had its `ra` save elided by `skip-ra` and looped back into itself on return. Branch bodies are checked the tail-aware way (`rv-body-needs-ra`, so a self tail call still costs nothing); the scrutinee is checked the ordinary way. ARM64 answers True for any match here, which is safe but saves `ra` for every match loop; this is the precise version.

author: fester
body: Name resolution: first match among the DEFINITIONS, with a leading runtime registration skipped when a definition of the same name exists. The fourth parameter is the runtime/definition boundary stamped into `runtime-funcs` by `rv-emit-module`; the ARM64 chapter carries the full account and the two measurements that forced this exact shape. A caller passing 0 gets plain first-match.
